title: Lulu and the Star Stepping Game
markdown:
In a meadow where the grass grew soft and the flowers bowed their sleepy heads toward night, lived a little lamb named Lulu. Her wool was the lightest lamb’s wool, white and puffy as a cloud, and her legs loved to hop. When the sun dipped low and painted the sky in orange, pink, and rosy gold, Lulu leaped and twirled. She leaped so high her wool tickled her nose. She twirled until the world spun in a delightful blur, and her hooves made little whispers on the grass, as if they were sharing tiny secrets with the earth. A moth might drift past her ear. A clover might brush her knee. Lulu would bleat a happy little bleat and hop again, because hopping was the way her joy came out.

Beside a patch of sweet clover, moving with a steady rhythm that matched the evening’s slow hum, was Cress the turtle. Her shell was like a polished stone, cool and smooth, patched with green moss. She watched the world with calm eyes that had seen many seasons. Lulu, full of light happy energy, would bound right past her, a swirl of white wool and little bleats, her tail a tiny flag. Oh, Cress, Lulu would call, breathless from dancing. Why are you so slow. The world is so exciting right now. You must dance. You must leap and play.

Cress would blink, unhurried as the meadow’s own breathing. Dancing is a lovely way to greet the world, little Lulu, she would say, her voice like leaves rustling. But so is watching. So is simply being here. The world is exciting in many ways, even when it is quiet and still.

One evening the last sliver of sun melted away like a drop of honey. The sky deepened to peaceful blue. Stars began to glimmer, tiny soft lights on a dark cloth. Lulu still felt lively, yet her leaps had gone wobbly and her twirls were no longer steady. Oh dear, she murmured, lying down on the cool grass with a sigh that stirred her wool. I feel all wiggly and jiggly inside, but my legs don’t want to dance. They feel tired, even though I still want to play. I wish I could be still, like you, Cress. I don’t know how to make the wiggles stop. A tiny line appeared between her brows.

Cress moved closer, as unhurried as twilight itself, and settled beside Lulu, her shell a comforting presence. It is perfectly all right to feel wiggly when you are ready for rest, she said gently. Sometimes the best games are the quietest ones, the ones that help busy thoughts settle like leaves drifting down. Would you like to play a bedtime game with me. It is called Star Stepping, and it helps little ones find their calm.

Lulu’s ears perked. Under her wool the wiggles still fluttered, like tiny moths. Star Stepping, she whispered. Is it a fast game. Does it involve lots of jumping.

It is as slow and as peaceful as you wish it to be, Cress replied, her eyes twinkling with the first stars. We will pretend the stars are little soft pebbles scattered across the sky. We will imagine stepping from one gentle star to another, but we will only take a step when we take a slow, soft breath. Ready to try.

Lulu nodded, doing her very best to quiet her lively legs. Cress closed her eyes a moment, a little smile on her ancient face. First, she murmured, we take a deep breath in, as if we are smelling the sweetest flower in the whole meadow. Lulu breathed in. Cool evening air filled her lungs: clover, damp earth, the faint sweetness of night. Now, Cress continued, like a lullaby, we let it out, slow and steady, like blowing a dandelion puff so softly that not a single seed falls too quickly. And with that breath, we take one tiny, gentle step.

And so they began. At first Lulu found it hard. Her breaths wanted to be quick little puffs. Her feet wanted to hop and skip. One hoof lifted too soon and she had to set it down again, giggling a tiny embarrassed giggle. Cress did not hurry her. Cress’s calm voice held her steady, an anchor in the flowing river of the night. Breathe in, little lamb, she murmured. And out, slow and soft. Imagine your feet barely touching the ground, just brushing a shimmering moonbeam. Feel the quiet grow inside you.

They took another step, and another. A cricket sang somewhere in the clover. The air cooled against Lulu’s wool. She could hear her own breath now, in and out, like a tiny tide. The stars did not move, but in her mind they made a path, pebble to pebble, silver to silver, each one waiting politely until she was ready.

Breath after slow breath, step after gentle step, something wonderful happened. The wiggles softened, melting like snowflakes in sun. The fluttery restless feeling smoothed into calm. Each breath was a little wave washing over busy mind and restless legs. Lulu imagined starlight under her hooves, shimmery paths through the quiet sky. She was not dancing, but she was moving. She was not leaping, but she was learning a new gentle way of being.

From the tall trees a distant owl called, a soft sleepy sound settling in for the night. Lulu did not look up. She took another slow breath, another soft step. The wiggles were almost gone. Her eyes felt heavy, like velvet curtains closing. She looked at Cress, who moved with the same peaceful grace she always did, her shell catching moonlight like a polished jewel. Being slow and steady felt warm and safe, like a woolly blanket woven from moonlight and dreams. The quiet game had not been boring. It had been wonderfully, deeply peaceful.

Thank you, Cress, Lulu whispered, barely louder than the crickets. She yawned a big stretchy yawn that loosened her from ears to hooves. The stars seemed to wink, as if they had been waiting for her to find this slower game. She lay down beside Cress, her fluffy wool a pillow for her sleepy head. Cress’s shell was cool against her side. The clover smelled sweet. The meadow was quiet. The night was calm. Lulu the lamb, who had once known only the joy of dancing, now knew the gentle magic of Star Stepping. With moonlight on her face and slow breaths still in her heart, she drifted into slumber, dreaming of starlight paths that never asked her to hurry.
